t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: This lecture is devoted to the examination of biological traces. Traces of blood, saliva, sweat and other secretions serve as physical evidence in solving grave crimes such as murder and rape. The group identity of blood is determined by the erythrocyte, serum, leukocyte and enzyme systems. The serum isosystems include immunoglobulin, that is Gm, haptoglobin, that is Hp, and the group-specific component, that is Gc. Saliva is identified by the enzyme amylase, and sweat by the amino acid serine. The lecture considers these methods.

t: The concept of physical evidence
n: The concept of physical evidence. According to Article 203 of the Criminal Procedure Code, physical evidence is an object bearing signs and features that make it possible to establish its origin, ownership and purpose. Physical evidence includes the instrument of the crime and objects that have preserved traces of the crime or were the object of criminal acts. Objects that serve to refute the charge or mitigate guilt are also considered physical evidence. Attention: forensic medical examination of evidence is not assigned to clinical doctors. They may be involved only in locating and describing evidence at the scene and in taking samples.

t: Biological physical evidence and laboratories
n: Biological evidence includes tissue fragments, blood, saliva, urine, sweat, semen, faeces, their stains, and hair. It is examined by specially trained specialists in the appropriate laboratory units. The distribution among laboratories is as follows: blood and semen stains are examined in the forensic biology department. Sections of organs and tissues go to the forensic histology department, identification of traces, bullets and persons to medical criminalistics, and detection of toxic substances to forensic chemistry.

t: The doctor's role at the scene
n: The doctor's role at the scene. Forensic medical examination of physical evidence is not assigned to clinical doctors. In some cases general practitioners and other doctors may be involved. They take part in examining the scene, in locating and describing evidence, and in taking samples for examination. Remember: the doctor finds the evidence and takes the sample, but the laboratory examination is carried out by forensic biology specialists. That is, finding is not the same as examining.

t: Case analysis: biological evidence found
n: Case analysis. At the scene, stains resembling blood were found on the wall and on a pillowcase. A doctor has been involved in the inspection. By law, physical evidence, including blood traces, is collected from the scene by the investigator; if necessary, doctors are involved. A small item, that is the pillowcase, is taken whole. From a hard surface, a scraping of the dry stain is taken, and from a clean area, a control sample. Question: how will you take a sample from the stain on the wall, and why is a control from an uncontaminated area needed?

t: Types of blood traces
n: Types of blood traces. A pool forms on poorly absorbent material and when there is a large amount of blood. A saturation stain appears on material that absorbs moisture well. A run-off trace is left by blood flowing down an inclined surface. Spatter traces occur with a sharp swing, a blow, or a fountain from an artery. A smear forms when a bloodied object slides over a hard surface. Attention: a smear is not an imprint. An imprint is left by contact without sliding, and its shape matches the surface of the object. Pools, saturation stains and run-off traces depend on the type of material and the bleeding.

t: Shape of a blood-drop stain
n: The shape of a blood-drop stain depends on the conditions of falling. On a horizontal surface, a stain from a drop falling from a height of 10–15 cm is round, with smooth edges. On an inclined surface, or when dripping from a moving part of the body, the stain is pear-shaped, like an exclamation mark; the narrow end points in the direction of movement. If the height of fall is greater, the edges are finely serrated. At a still greater height, spatters, that is secondary stains, appear around it. Spatters lie mainly in the direction of movement or on the lower side of the surface.

t: Collecting blood traces for forensic examination
n: A blood trace is collected from the scene by the investigator; if necessary, doctors are also involved. The choice depends on the size of the object. Small items such as clothing, footwear, weapons and bed sheets are taken to the laboratory whole. From a large object, that is a tapestry, carpet or mattress, the stained piece is cut out. A piece from an unstained and uncontaminated area is taken as a control; that is, a control piece is also taken from a clean area.

t: Sampling from hard surfaces, snow and soil
n: New gauze or bandage is not recommended: the dressing agent adversely affects serological reactions. Pieces of gauze are dried indoors, in a place out of the sun and not next to a heater, and wrapped separately. From a pool of blood, less than 10 ml is taken into a vial; if that is difficult, a 4 by 4 cm piece of gauze is soaked. The method is chosen according to the substrate. From a hard surface, a scraping of the dry stain is taken with a scalpel, and the same kind of scraping from a clean area. For a wash, the area is wiped with damp gauze, 2 by 2 cm. Snow is put into a container and melted indoors. Soil and sand are taken whole onto a plate and dried. In each case a control is taken in the same way from a clean place.

t: Quick question: sampling rules
n: Quick question. Why is a sample taken not only from the area with the blood stain but also from an uncontaminated area? Answer: this is the control sample. It is taken in the same way for scrapings, washes, snow, soil and fabric pieces. New gauze or bandage is not recommended for sampling: the chemical dressings in them adversely affect serological reactions. Attention, there is a risk of error: the object under examination and the control sample are never sent in the same package.

t: Sequence of tasks in blood examination
n: The tasks of blood examination are solved in a strict order. First, the presence of blood. Second, species origin. Third, group identity. Fourth, attribution to a specific person. Sometimes sex, regional origin, and attribution to a pregnant woman or one who has recently given birth are also requested. The examinations are carried out in the forensic biology departments of forensic medical examination institutions.

t: Presumptive methods for detecting blood
n: Presumptive methods for detecting blood. The peroxide, benzidine and phenolphthalein tests are based on the blood enzymes peroxidase and catalase. When a 3% solution of hydrogen peroxide is dropped on, white foam forms. Benzidine gives a blue colour with peroxide. Phenolphthalein with 3% peroxide gives a pinkish colour in 10–15 seconds. When luminol is sprayed or dropped on, a light-blue glow is visible for up to 1 minute. In ultraviolet light the stain is dark brown and velvety; in an old stain a fiery fluorescence is seen. Attention: the tests are non-specific and may give false positives; they only raise suspicion of blood.

t: Confirmatory methods for detecting blood
n: Confirmatory methods for detecting blood: microscopic, microcrystalline, spectral and chromatographic examinations. In the microscopic method erythrocytes are found, but its possibilities are limited. In the microcrystalline method haemoglobin crystals are viewed; its sensitivity is low and it is not used. In the spectral method, wave absorption is determined with a microspectral microscope. The chromatographic method uses paper or Silufol, and it is now the main method. Attention: a presumptive method is not a confirmatory one. A presumptive test does not prove blood conclusively; it only allows suspicion.

t: Determining the species origin of blood
n: The species origin of blood. Whether a blood stain is human or animal is decided by determining species origin. In the Chistovich–Ulengut method, serum is added to the extract: in the tube with serum against human protein, a precipitation ring appears. Electrophoresis on cellulose acetate is used when there is little blood in the extract, with species-specific sera. The Ouchterlony method is used when the extract is turbid, and precipitation is observed in agar gel. The ABAcard test makes it possible to learn the presence of blood and the species at the same time: it shows the presence of blood and human origin.

t: Case analysis: what does the blood stain show
n: Case analysis. At the scene, when 3% hydrogen peroxide was dropped on a stain on the wall, white foam formed. What can be said: there is a high probability of blood in the stain, so the examination is directed to this stain; the test allows suspicion. What cannot be said: the test is non-specific and may give a false positive, so the presence of blood cannot be stated conclusively. Question: in the sequence of the examination, that is blood, species, group, person, which is the next step and by what method is it carried out?

t: Blood group systems
n: Blood group systems are divided into four types: erythrocyte, serum, leukocyte and enzyme systems. The erythrocyte systems include ABO, Rhesus, MNSs and Lewis. The serum systems include Gm, Hp and Gc. The enzyme systems include acid phosphatase, phosphoglucomutase and others. The leukocyte system is the HLA antigen system. By these, the number of antigens and their combinations exceeds several hundred thousand. The examination usually begins with study of the ABO erythrocyte system.

t: Serum isosystems: Gm, Hp, Gc
n: The serum isosystems include the systems of immunoglobulin, that is Gm, haptoglobin, that is Hp, and the group-specific component, that is Gc. The Gm system is tested in blood together with the Lewis system and helps to determine secretor status. Secretors make up about 80% of people. In them, blood group antigens are also found in secretions such as semen, urine and saliva. When comparing a blood trace with a person's blood, after ABO, if necessary, antigens of other systems are also tested.

t: Enzyme systems and HLA
n: The enzyme systems include erythrocyte acid phosphatase, phosphoglucomutase and cholinesterase. The adenylate kinase and 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase systems are also among the enzyme group systems. There is also the leukocyte antigen system, that is HLA. Two persons cannot have absolutely identical antigens across all group systems. At present, a person is conclusively identified by DNA examination.

t: The ABO system: difference between medicine and forensic medicine
n: The ABO system is tested differently in medicine and in forensic medicine. Forensic medical examination of blood group usually begins with study of the ABO erythrocyte system. In medical institutions only the agglutinogens of the ABO system are tested, and the agglutinins are not. In forensic medicine both agglutinogens and agglutinins are tested. Attention: ABO is not final; if necessary, antigens of other systems are then also tested.

t: Determining the group in liquid blood and in a blood stain
n: Determining the group in liquid blood and in a blood stain. In liquid blood, the Schiff method is used: the blood is centrifuged, the serum and formed elements are separated, agglutinogens are determined with anti-A and anti-B, and agglutinins with standard erythrocytes. In a stain, for agglutinogens, absorption, its quantitative variant, absorption-elution and mixed agglutination reactions are used. If the stain is small or the antigens are weak, the absorption-elution reaction is recommended. In a stain, agglutinins are determined with a mixture of standard erythrocytes by the cover-glass method, that is the Lattes method.

t: Quick question: isosystems and ABO
n: Quick questions. Which systems belong to the serum isosystems? Answer: immunoglobulin, that is Gm, haptoglobin, that is Hp, and the group-specific component, that is Gc. Which erythrocyte system do forensic examinations usually begin with? Answer: the ABO system. What does the Lattes method determine in a stain? Answer: agglutinins, with the help of standard erythrocytes. Attention: ABO, Rhesus, MNSs and Lewis are erythrocyte systems; Gm, Hp and Gc are serum isosystems. Do not confuse them.

t: Attribution of blood to a specific person
n: Attribution of blood to a specific person. Blood traces from the scene are compared with the suspect's own blood by group systems. The examination usually begins with the ABO system. If necessary, antigens of other systems are also tested. In two people, antigens across all group systems cannot coincide completely. Such a comparison requires much labour and time. Therefore DNA examination is now used more often.

t: DNA examination: a modern possibility
n: DNA examination is a modern possibility. In recent times, the attribution of blood to a specific person has been established conclusively by means of DNA examination. In 1985, A. Jeffreys stated that the study of DNA polymorphism could be important in forensic biology, and from 1986 genetic methods began to be used. The method is also called genomic fingerprinting, genotyping and DNA analysis. Its essence is determining each person's genetic characteristics. DNA regions located at the same place on a pair of chromosomes and responsible for one trait are called homologous loci.

t: Blood features: sex, region, pregnancy, age
n: Additional features of blood. Sex is determined by X and Y chromatin: Y chromatin stains with acriquine and is visible under fluorescence microscopy; in a man Y, in a woman X chromatin, and DNA is also possible. For regional origin, epithelial cells of mucous membranes are examined: nose, lung, intestine, uterus, vagina. From blood, pregnancy is determined by chorionic gonadotropic hormone; it cannot be conclusively determined from a blood stain. A feature of age: in adults the blood contains haemoglobin HbA, in infants fetal haemoglobin HbF; HbF is more resistant to alkali. This is determined in a fresh stain; in one 15–20 days old it is absent.

t: Assessing the age and quantity of a blood trace
n: The age of a blood trace is assessed from the change in haemoglobin and the fall in blood enzyme activity. Attention, there is a risk of error: this assessment is not an exact date, but only an approximate conclusion. Changes in the trace depend not only on age: temperature, humidity, wind and the properties of the object bearing the stain also have an effect. The quantity of blood shed outward, if needed, is assessed taking into account that one litre of liquid blood leaves on average about 210 g of dry residue.

t: Case analysis: the group matched
n: Case analysis. A blood stain at the scene matched the suspect's blood in the ABO system. Question: can it be stated conclusively that the stain belongs to the suspect? The stain and the person's blood are compared by group systems. One usually begins with the ABO system and, if necessary, tests antigens of other systems. Attention, risk of error: a match in one system does not mean a match in all systems. In two persons antigens across all systems do not coincide completely. Such a comparison requires much labour and time. In recent times, the attribution of blood to a specific person has been established conclusively by DNA examination.

t: Examination of semen traces: tasks to be solved
n: In forensic medical examination of semen traces, four tasks are solved: first, the presence of semen; second, species origin; third, group identity; fourth, attribution to a specific person. As with blood, there are presumptive and confirmatory methods for determining the presence of semen. In most cases the question of the species origin of semen is not put to the examination; it is needed very rarely. Species origin is resolved by the morphological method, from the shape and size of the spermatozoon, and by other methods, with the precipitation reaction.

t: Methods for detecting semen
n: Methods for detecting semen. Presumptive methods: microcrystalline reactions, that is Florence and Barberio, which now have no practical importance; the potato juice reaction; ultraviolet light. Semen inhibits the property of potato juice to agglutinate erythrocytes; if there is inhibition, the reaction is positive. In ultraviolet light a semen stain gives a pale light-blue fluorescence; on synthetic fabrics this is difficult, because the fabric itself may fluoresce. The confirmatory method is morphological: if at least one whole spermatozoon, that is head, body and tail together, is found, the result is positive. In azoospermia and necrospermia, paper chromatography is used: if choline, spermine and acid phosphatase are found together, semen is reliably established.

t: Group of semen and attribution to a person
n: The group identity of semen is determined, as for blood, by group factors; the ABO system is most often tested. In rape and sodomy cases the stain may also contain antigens from the victim's vaginal or rectal secretions. For this reason, together with the stain material, blood and saliva samples from the suspect and the victim are submitted for examination. Then the group factors are compared. In examination of a corpse, blood and bile are taken to the laboratory to determine secretor status.

t: Saliva and sweat as objects of examination
n: Objects for saliva examination: cigarette butt, handkerchief, towel, envelope and stamp, dishes, a piece of cloth used as a gag, bitten food. When collecting the object, rubber gloves are put on, and small items are taken with forceps. The presence of saliva is determined by the enzyme amylase. For sweat, clothing, footwear, bedding and towels are most often taken. Sweat contains a lot of the amino acid serine, and sweat in a stain is identified by it. Attention, there is a risk of error: the object under examination and the control object must not be in one package. They are wrapped separately, in a dried state.

t: Detecting the presence of saliva: amylase
n: Traces of saliva are sought on cigarette butts, handkerchiefs, towels, envelopes, dishes and pieces of cloth used as a gag. The presence of saliva is resolved by determining the salivary enzyme, that is amylase. The procedure is as follows: find the object, take it with gloves and forceps, determine the enzyme amylase, dry at room temperature in the shade, wrap separately and send. Attention: the object and the control sample must not be in one package; dry them away from sun and heat.

t: Detecting the presence of sweat: serine
n: In examination of sweat, clothing, footwear, bedding and towels are most often taken as objects of examination. Sweat contains a large amount of the amino acid serine. The question of whether sweat is present in a stain is resolved precisely by determining this amino acid. Remember: saliva is identified by amylase, sweat by serine. The species origin of sweat and saliva is determined very rarely; the group is usually found by the ABO system, that is the blood group system.

t: Comparing urine and faecal stains
n: Urine and faecal stains are examined relatively rarely in practice, mainly in connection with sexual offences. In faeces, the proteins that act as antigen are broken down, so species and group are not determined. Urine has no species-specific protein, so species is not determined; the group, however, is found by the ABO system. For comparison: in urine, creatinine and urea are determined by a chemical method. In faeces, food, micro-organisms and helminth eggs are seen by microscopic examination. The species and group identity of faeces cannot be established, because the antigen is broken down.

t: Species and group identity of secretions
n: Determination of species origin in a saliva or sweat stain is required very rarely; if needed, species-specific sera are used. The group identity of saliva, sweat and urine is usually determined by the ABO blood group system. According to the table: in saliva and sweat, species origin is rarely determined, with species serum, and the group is determined. In urine, species is not determined, and the group is determined. In faeces, neither is determined. Attention: in urine species is not determined; in faeces neither species nor group is determined.

t: Secretors and non-secretors
n: Secretors and non-secretors. In about 80% of people, blood group antigens are also found in saliva and other secretions; they are secretors. The rest are non-secretors. Secretor status is determined by the Lewis and Gm systems, that is immunoglobulin, in the blood. In the Lewis system, Le a minus b plus is a secretor, Le a plus b minus is a non-secretor, and Le a minus b minus cannot be clearly designated. From the suspect, blood and saliva are taken for comparison; saliva clarifies the question of secretor status.

t: Collecting, drying and sending the sample
n: Collecting, drying and sending the sample. Before the sample is taken, the mouth is rinsed and 2–3 ml of saliva is collected in a tube; if possible, it is taken in the forensic biology department. The saliva is centrifuged, the supernatant is applied to gauze, dried and wrapped in paper. Drying is at room temperature, away from the sun. The object and the control are wrapped separately, not in one package; they are dried away from sunlight and heat.

t: Quick question: sweat, saliva and packaging
n: Quick question. By which enzyme is saliva identified in a stain, and by which amino acid is sweat? What is determined in a urine stain? Answer: saliva by the enzyme amylase, sweat by the amino acid serine. In a urine stain, creatinine and urea are determined. Attention, risk of error: the object under examination and the control object are not put in one package. Each is wrapped separately. The objects are dried at room temperature: in a place not exposed to direct sunlight, away from a heat source, and where insects cannot get in.

t: Case analysis: examination of saliva and sweat
n: Case analysis. A cigarette butt was found at the scene, and the victim's clothing has a suspicious stain. Question: which method, what conclusion? A cigarette butt is regarded as a saliva object. It is taken with forceps, wearing rubber gloves. Saliva is determined by amylase. The presence of sweat in the stain on the clothing is resolved by determining the amino acid serine; clothing is a frequently collected object for sweat. Conclusion: species origin is needed very rarely; if needed, species-specific sera are used. Group identity is usually determined by the ABO system.

t: Conclusion and main errors
n: Main conclusion: saliva is identified by amylase, sweat by serine, and urine by creatinine and urea. The group of saliva, sweat and urine is usually determined by the ABO system. A presumptive method is distinguished from a confirmatory one. Taking blood as the example, presumptive tests are non-specific and give only suspicion, whereas the reliable method is chromatography. Typical errors: wrapping the control together with the object; trying to determine species in urine, and species and group in faeces. Review questions: how are saliva and sweat identified? Which items are saliva objects? How are samples dried and wrapped?
